faq.q: What is the flare when landing?
faq.a: The flare is the small nose-up movement just before touchdown. It slows the rate of descent so the plane settles onto its main wheels instead of hitting the runway nose first.
asks: Why does the nose go up just before landing?

faq.q: How do pilots find the runway in fog?
faq.a: An instrument landing system sends two radio beams from the runway: one shows left or right, the other the correct slope. Following them, specially equipped planes can even land automatically in thick fog.
Doors or panels on the engine turn the fan's air forwards instead of backwards. This helps slow the plane on the runway, especially when it is wet or slippery.
asks: Why do engines get loud after landing?

faq.q: Why do some landings feel firm?
faq.a: On wet or short runways pilots touch down firmly on purpose. A positive landing pushes through water to grip the runway and gets the brakes working quickly, so it is safe, not a mistake.
asks: Was a bumpy landing a bad landing?

faq.q: Why do planes land into the wind?
faq.a: Landing into a headwind lets the plane keep its normal airspeed while moving slower over the ground. That shortens the landing roll and makes the plane easier to control.

facts: A standard instrument approach descends at about 3 degrees, losing roughly 300 feet of height per nautical mile.
Airliners with the right equipment can make fully automatic landings, called autoland, in fog.

quiz.why: Spoilers spoil the wing's lift, putting the plane's weight on its wheels so the brakes grip.

wrong.1: Spoilers reduce lift; they never help a plane climb.
wrong.2: They sit on top of the wings, far from the brakes, and their job is to kill lift.
